overview: This file concerns the severe rise in the cost of living in postwar Korea and the information supplied by the U.S. Department of State to Lee A. Terrill of the International Committee of Young Men’s Christian Associations. A departmental memorandum and the resulting reply report that Korea’s December 1948 wholesale price index stood at 70,000 with 1937 equal to 100, describe the change in the dollar exchange rate from 3.47 to 1 in 1937 to an official military rate of 450 to 1 in October 1948, and compare Seoul open-market prices with government commissary and U.S. prices. They also discuss foreign-exchange licensing, customs duties, household-effects exemptions, and the implications of Korean consumption patterns for foreign missionaries.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Terrill on living costs and exchange rates in Korea
subfiles.from: Leonard R. Cowles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Lee A. Terrill, International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations
subfiles.about: The State Department answers Terrill’s request for information on Korean living costs, currency exchange, and import regulations affecting Americans and missionaries.
subfiles.summary: The letter reports a December 1948 Korean cost-of-living proxy—actually the Bank of Korea’s Seoul wholesale price index—of 70,000 when 1937 equals 100; the page-one OCR value “0.00000” is an obvious error corrected by the supporting memorandum. It gives an average 1937 dollar exchange rate of 3.47 to 1 and an October 1948 official military rate of 450 to 1, while noting that other transactions lacked an established rate. Seoul open-market prices for Americans without commissary access were estimated at 25–50 percent above commissary prices and 15–40 percent above prices in New York or Washington. The letter also describes foreign-exchange licensing, exemptions for reasonable quantities of personal and household effects, and a 10-percent ad valorem duty on nonexempt goods.

subfiles.title: Lydman memorandum supplying information for the Terrill reply
subfiles.about: Lydman provides the economic figures and regulatory information used to prepare the Department’s response to Terrill.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies the December 1948 Korean index as 70,000 relative to a 1937 base of 100 and explains that it was the Bank of Korea’s simple geometric mean for 80 commodities. It warns that an index based on Korean consumption would not precisely represent the expenses of foreign missionaries. It also supplies the 1937 and 1948 exchange rates, describes the Korean Foreign Exchange Bank’s ad hoc licensing role, compares Seoul market prices with commissary and U.S. prices, and summarizes customs treatment inherited from the American Military Government.

interest: The file offers unusually concise quantitative evidence of the scale of Korean wartime and postwar inflation, with the wholesale price index reaching 70,000 on a 1937 base of 100. It is also useful for showing how official exchange rates, commissary access, and differing consumption patterns complicated comparisons between Korean and expatriate living costs. The memorandum and finished reply together reveal how the State Department translated internal economic reporting into practical guidance for a missionary organization during the transition from American military rule to the new Korean government.
